title: What are your thoughts on Fitzcarraldo?

commenti.body:
I can't see anyone else in that role. The great Kinski roles are the ones where I couldn't see anyone else doing it. I loved Fitzcarraldo every time I've seen it, it has a strange endearing quality, maybe stemming from Kinski's performance, maybe from the brutal realism of Herzog. 

I like Aguirre the most from the Herzog&Kinski collab. I just like the setting more and it plays to Kinski's unhinged craziness even more.  

I also recommend Nosferatu and Woyzeck. Cobra Verde is the only one I haven't seen.

I know little of the crew and movie in general when I watched this and still know little. But its a great poem of craziness and I for sure enjoy "watching a movie crew make a film to lift a boat" more than "watching a film about lift a boat".

The motives are complex , in the film and the making of. But its distilled and striped by the jungle , making the result almost like a child story book

And no Nicholson cant take this shit , he is sane

Last week I watched the documentary about the making of Fitzcarraldo, 'The Burden of Dreams'. When it mentioned how Jagger and Robard were in the initial version of the film, then had to be cut because of illness and prior engagements, I couldn't help putting on my tinfoil hat. The footage of them in the lead roles is not convincing to me at all. They both seem miscast. If it strikes me like that, obviously Herzog would have been well aware of this too, so maybe they were removed from the project and a cover story was concocted. Kinski obviously makes the lead role his own.

Lately, I've been enamored by these huge productions that were only made because the directors were absolutely crazy. I watched Friedkin's _Sorcerer_ and fell in love with it. _Heaven's Gate_ is next in queue and a rewatch of _Apocalypse Now_ is in order. I guess I'll be rewatching _Fitzcarraldo_ as well. 

I have nothing insightful to say about the film itself but are these kind of movies made anymore? I'd love to see some examples of recent films fitting the bill.

I feel like it's a broadly poetic film. The goal seems so absurd and so incredibly demanding that no explanation of it will suffice. The question itself, "why," is consumed by the sheer scale of effort and cost, and I begin to think that he'd simply better stop, or that he'd damn well better succeed. An unforgettable film, to be sure, although I enjoyed Burden of Dreams much more.
Were these directors crazy, or just naive? They didn't have the benefit of watching Burden of Dreams or Heart of Darkness.

I've got *one* recent*ish* film.

Whenever I try to sell someone on Hard to be a God (Aleksei German, 2013), I say something like "it's the most impressive film I've ever seen, and I've seen Fitzcarraldo".

 It took two generations of a family to complete the film, over thirteen or more years. Where Fitzcarraldo went big in one scene, Hard to be a God goes dense in every scene.

It's a brutal 3 hour slog through medieval mud and misery. One of my top 3 films, and I've only watched it from start to finish once in the decade that I've known about it.

It's up for free on YouTube.
That's recent for sure! Even though it was several years in the making. Thank you for the heads up!

An incredible film-- I sincerely can barely believe it was ever made. A testament to the mad dreams of Werner Herzog, and man in general. The film is almost a metaphor for his career. 

I wish it wasn't dubbed, though.

Herzog is a genius, even his not-so-good films are worth watching, considering, and maybe rewatching. I recently read this memoir and it seems like Fitzcarraldo is either his proudest achievement, or at least the experience of making it is the thing that haunts him most. Possibly both. I believe that the story is secondary to the achievement both in the film and in the production.
I can only recommend to watch the "making of" documentary *Burden of Dreams* and you'll appreciate the movie even more.

I *just* watched Fitzcarraldo for the first time last night. Amazing movie. It's hard to imagine anyone but Kinski being able to portray Fitzgerald's desperate obsession with opera & Caruso. The scene at the party where he puts on the phonograph and looks around *so confidently* expecting everyone there to be struck dumb by the magnificence of the music. You can't help but feel sorry for him when *no one* (except maybe his entourage of local children) seems to get anywhere near the same feelings of ecstasy from the sounds of opera.  
  
Immediately after finishing *Fitzcarraldo* I watched *My Best Fiend*, Herzog's film about his and Kinski's relationship. It's wild how different some of the perspectives were. The women who acted opposite Kinski in *Fitzcarraldo* and *Wocyzek* described him as a consummate professional, kind and sensitive. I have to believe they were trying to soften the viewer's impression in the face of the very damning footage of Kinski screaming at production managers about the food on set being bad. But Herzog kept going back to work with him. I think he even said it in the movie, he and Kinski kind of needed each other, maybe even fed each other. No one ever seemed to call Kinski's behavior out as signs of mental illness, even though that seems glaringly obvious.  

  
Regardless, it seems Kinski & Herzog made incredible films together. *Fitzcarraldo* was my first, and I look forward to seeing the rest.
Your theory is very plausible.

One of Herzog's Bergfilms, in a sense. So much of his work deals with man's defiance of gravity, and how that innate struggle drives us to extreme ends. For a filmography filled with incredulous ascents and mountain climbs, the steamboat sliding up a hill is certainly the crown jewel of them. 

If you're looking for more Kinski I think Cobra Verde is especially underrated.
If you haven't, add On the Silver Globe to your list, and the documentary, Escape to the Silver Globe.

The story reminds me of Sisyphus, both in its cyclical (and futile) nature and the craziness of Sisyphus/Fitz. Except that we don't need to imagine Fitzcarraldo happy; he was at the end.

I don't know if I am reading too much into the film or not, as not many other aspects suggests this. It's probably not that deep, and on its own, as a spectacle of how determined a person can be to achieve their dreams, it's already a great film.

Cobra Verde is good, you should definitely check it out if you liked the others. I will say that it has a somewhat disjointed feel, as Herzog spends quite a bit of time showing the native people simply going about their lives. You can tell from the film that Herzog's inner documentarian is about to emerge

Fitzcarraldo is more interesting as performance art than as a movie. Not that's it's not a good movie or something, just not as great as Herzog's other work. It kind of feels like a lesser version of Aguirre to me.

I think it's a weirdly positive movie for Herzog. His films are usually about the harshness of nature and the crazy people who think they can tame it. And while it has elements of that, it's main message is that this one man was crazy enough to be able to tame nature, and how uplifting that was. It really made me feel "oh you can follow and complete a crazy dream"
It's awesome that just the other day I got a copy of _On the Silver Globe_! I haven't watched it yet, but I'm adding it to the list. Thanks!
Exactly, it's a strangely optimistic and life-affirming movie. I think that juxtaposition is why I like it so much.

The documentary is more interesting than the film. And it has one of the funniest scenes in human history: [”The birds doesn’t sing, they just screech in pain”](https://youtu.be/3xQyQnXrLb0?si=qT_3-enP08D1xuut)
